stem: Calculate the spin only magnetic moment of divalent cation of a transition metal with atomic number 25.
solution:
For element with atomic number 25, electronic configuration for its divalent cation will be

\(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^5\ 4s^0}\)  — the five 3d electrons occupy the five 3d orbitals singly and the 4s orbital is empty.

There are 5 unpaired electrons, so \(n = 5\).

\(\therefore \mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\) BM

stem: Which of the following will have highest fourth ionization enthalpy \(\mathrm{IE_4}\)? \(\mathrm{La^{4\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{Gd^{4\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{Lu^{4\oplus}}\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed solution box stops at the method and never says which ion actually has the highest \(\mathrm{IE_4}\) — the conclusion below is supplied. Table 8.12 compounds the gap: it is captioned "First, second, third and fourth ionization enthalpies of lanthanoids" but prints only the \(\mathrm{IE_1}\), \(\mathrm{IE_2}\) and \(\mathrm{IE_3}\) columns, so the \(\mathrm{IE_4}\) values this question asks about appear nowhere in the chapter.]

First write electronic configuration of that element/ion. Check for any unpaired electrons present. The energy required for removal of that electron will be less as compared to the energy required to remove an electron from an electron pair. Also compare the energies of the orbitals occupying those electrons. It will be easier to remove an electron from an orbital that is lower in energy than the one with higher in energy. First ionization enthalpy generally decrease across the period.

Applying that method to the three ions:

\(\mathrm{La^{3\oplus} = [Xe]\ 4f^0}\) — the bare xenon core, a closed noble-gas shell.

\(\mathrm{Gd^{3\oplus} = [Xe]\ 4f^7}\) — an exactly half-filled 4f subshell.

\(\mathrm{Lu^{3\oplus} = [Xe]\ 4f^{14}}\) — a completely filled 4f subshell.

\(\mathrm{IE_4}\) is the energy needed to pull the fourth electron out of each of these tripositive ions. All three are stable arrangements, but the noble-gas core of \(\mathrm{La^{3\oplus}}\) is the most stable of the three, and its remaining electrons lie in the compact, strongly bound xenon shell rather than in an outer 4f subshell. Removing an electron from it is therefore the hardest.

\(\therefore\) **lanthanum has the highest fourth ionization enthalpy** of the three.
